pebbles.title: FloodNet ultrasonic depth sensors (NYC)

narration.short: FloodNet sensors and historical flood events near this address.

provenance.source_name: FloodNet (New York University and The City University of New York)
provenance.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
provenance.citation: FloodNet street flood sensors. Flood events and sensor status read from the FloodNet Data API (api.floodnet.nyc, an early-access beta) at the retrieval time shown. A flood event is a series of depth measurements greater than 10 mm at the sensor (FloodNet's definition); a depth is measured at one point and does not show the depth on every part of the street. Riprap counts the events the API marks as verified by a person. FloodNet's published cautions about a depth: "most FloodNet sensors are mounted over sidewalks and are thus unable to measure floods in the roadbed until the water rises above the height of the curb"; the depth at the street's lowest point differs from the reading by the sensor's height above that point; "a single anomalous data point, measured during a flood event" may exaggerate a maximum depth; and a sensor may miss a flood "if it was offline and awaiting repair or had not been deployed yet or retired" (FloodNet's NYC Open Data description, dataset aq7i-eu5q). Ten rows of FloodNet's deployments table are NOAA and USGS tide gauges (deploy_type "tidal"); Riprap does not count them as FloodNet sensors. Riprap names no sensor, because FloodNet's licence forbids reposting its records: each verified event can be found by its date and depth in FloodNet's own table on NYC Open Data, "FloodNet: Street Flooding Events Measured by FloodNet Sensors" (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/aq7i-eu5q), and on its dashboard (https://dataviz.floodnet.nyc). (2022), Water Research, 118648, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2022.118648. dep_extreme_2080.narrative: The city's stormwater flood map "Extreme Flood (3.66 inches/hr) with 2080 Sea Level Rise" shows no flooding category, at the edge of flooding mapped on it (within about 4 m) at the point mapped for this address. The city's stormwater flood maps are modelled scenarios (each a design storm paired with a sea level), not forecasts: their rainfall flooding categories cover public areas and rain only, the city says the map "does not provide the exact depth of flooding at any location", and it is not a flood plain determination. The city's Stormwater Resiliency Plan (2021) calls its moderate storm "the 10-year storm, with approximately 10 percent chance of occurrence in any given year" and its extreme storm "the 100-year storm, with approximately 1 percent chance of occurrence in any given year". Outside a mapped extent does not mean safe: NYC Emergency Management reports that during Hurricane Ida in 2021 "The most heavily impacted areas, representing over half of all damaged buildings, were also outside of any flood risk scenario, including FEMA floodplain maps and the NYC Stormwater Resiliency Plan's Extreme and Moderate stormwater scenarios" (NYC Hazard Mitigation Plan, flooding profile, nychazardmitigation.com).

floodnet.title: FloodNet street flood sensors. Flood events and sensor status read from the FloodNet Data API (api.floodnet.nyc, an early-access beta) at the retrieval time shown. A flood event is a series of depth measurements greater than 10 mm at the sensor (FloodNet's definition); a depth is measured at one point and does not show the depth on every part of the street. Riprap counts the events the API marks as verified by a person. FloodNet's published cautions about a depth: "most FloodNet sensors are mounted over sidewalks and are thus unable to measure floods in the roadbed until the water rises above the height of the curb"; the depth at the street's lowest point differs from the reading by the sensor's height above that point; "a single anomalous data point, measured during a flood event" may exaggerate a maximum depth; and a sensor may miss a flood "if it was offline and awaiting repair or had not been deployed yet or retired" (FloodNet's NYC Open Data description, dataset aq7i-eu5q). Ten rows of FloodNet's deployments table are NOAA and USGS tide gauges (deploy_type "tidal"); Riprap does not count them as FloodNet sensors. Riprap names no sensor, because FloodNet's licence forbids reposting its records: each verified event can be found by its date and depth in FloodNet's own table on NYC Open Data, "FloodNet: Street Flooding Events Measured by FloodNet Sensors" (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/aq7i-eu5q), and on its dashboard (https://dataviz.floodnet.nyc).
